spans.s:
Śaśa, ‘hare,’ is found once in the Rigveda, where it is said to have swallowed a razor. The animal is occasionally mentioned later also.
Foot notes x. 28, 2. Later, a goat supplants the hare in this curious story; see Bo7thling, Proceedings of the Saxon Academy, 1894, et seq.
Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiii. 56; xxiv. 38; Maitrāyaṇī Samhitā, iii. 14, 15; the hare in the moon, Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, xi. 1, 5, 3.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 84.

Śāsa denotes in the Brāhmaṇas a ‘sword’ or ‘knife.’
Foot notes aitareya brāhmaṇa, vii. 17, 5; śāṅkhāyana śrauta sūtra, xv. 25, 1 (of the knife to be used in slaying śunaḥśepa); Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iii. 8, 1, 4, 5; xiii. 2, 3, 16.

Sasa in the Rigveda denotes ‘herb’ or ‘grass.’ The word is also applied to the soma plant and the sacrificial straw.
Foot notes i. 51, 3; x. 79, 3.
i. 51, 3; x. 79, 3.
iii. 5, 6; iv. 5, 7, etc.
v. 21, 4.

Śaśayu, ‘pursuing the hare,’ is the epithet of some animal (mṛga) in the Atharvaveda. Zimmer thinks the tiger is meant, but this is not likely. Roth considers that a bird of prey is intended, while Whitney, following the commentator, renders the word by ‘lurking.’
Foot notes iv. 3, 6.
Altindisches Leben, 79, 84.
In Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 149.
Loc. cit.
Cf. Bloomfield, Hymns of the Atharvaveda, 368.

Śaṣpa in the later Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas denotes ‘young or sprouting grass.’
Foot notes Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 13, 81; xxi. 29; aitareya brāhmaṇa, viii. 5, 3; 8, 4; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, xii. 7, 2, 8; 9, 1, 2, etc.
Śastṛ in the Rigveda (i. 162, 5) and the Atharvaveda (ix. 3, 3) denotes the slaughterer of an animal.

Śastra is the technical term for the ‘recitation’ of the hotṛ priest, as opposed to the stotra of the Udgātṛ. The recitations at the morning offering of soma are called the ājya and Praüga; at the midday offering, the Marutvatīya and the Niṣkevalya; at the evening offering, the Vaiśvadeva and the Āgnimāruta.
Foot notes taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 2, 7, 2, etc.; kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xxix. 2, etc.; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xix. 25. 28, etc.; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iv. 2, 4, 20, etc. Cf. Weber, Indische Studien, 10, 353, and Caland and Henry, L'Agniṣṭoma, passim, where the Śastras are set out at length.

Sasarparī is a word occurring in two curious verses of the Rigveda. According to a later interpretation, it designates a particular kind of skill in speech which viśvāmitra obtained from jamadagni. What it was is quite uncertain.
Foot notes iii. 53, 15, 16.
Bṛhaddevatā, iii. 113, with Macdonell's notes. Cf. Geldner, Vedische Studien, 2, 159.

Sasya in the Atharvaveda and later regularly denotes ‘corn’ generally. It corresponds to the Avestan hahya. See kṛṣi.
Foot notes vii. 11, 1; viii. 10, 24.
taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 4, 3, 3; v. 1, 7, 3; vii. 5, 20, 1; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 2, etc.
Cf. Schrader, Prehistoric Antiquities, 284.
